concept.title: Exponential Sums of GL(2) Fourier Coefficients with Double Weighting
concept.concept_description: Investigate an exponential sum of the form \(\sum_{n \le X} \sum_{m \le Y} a(n) b(m) c(n+m)\) where \(a, b\) are normalized GL(2) Fourier coefficients and \(c\) is a bounded arithmetic function, using partial results from Theorem 1.2 of the paper. The goal is to derive non-trivial cancellation bounds with a power saving over the classical \(X Y\) bound.
concept.mathematical_framing: Investigate an exponential sum of the form \(\sum_{n \le X} \sum_{m \le Y} a(n) b(m) c(n+m)\) where \(a, b\) are normalized GL(2) Fourier coefficients and \(c\) is a bounded arithmetic function, using partial results from Theorem 1.2 of the paper. The goal is to derive non-trivial cancellation bounds with a power saving over the classical \(X Y\) bound.
concept.lean_guess: Apply the circle method with character sum estimates, leveraging existing bounds on GL(2) coefficients and orthogonal decomposition of sums over \(m\) via Kloosterman decomposition.

concept.title: Sheared Witt vectors commute with filtered colimits of nilperfect rings
concept.concept_description: For any filtered diagram of nilperfect rings (rings whose reduction is a perfect F_p-algebra) the natural map from the filtered colimit of their sheared Witt vectors to the sheared Witt vectors of the colimit ring is an isomorphism of rings.
concept.mathematical_framing: For any filtered diagram of nilperfect rings (rings whose reduction is a perfect F_p-algebra) the natural map from the filtered colimit of their sheared Witt vectors to the sheared Witt vectors of the colimit ring is an isomorphism of rings.
concept.lean_guess: Show that the subfunctor hw(R) of nilpotent Witt vectors preserves filtered colimits, that the inverse limit lim_F (W(R)/hw(R)) also preserves filtered colimits (using the perfection of reductions and the fact that transition maps are Frobenius‑equivariant), and then deduce the result for chW(R) from the short exact sequence 0 → hw(R) → chW(R) → lim_F (W(R)/hw(R)) → 0.

concept.title: Vampire Numbers and Other Numerical Monsters: A Bestiary of Arithmetic Oddities
concept.concept_description: A vampire number is a composite number v with an even number of digits that can be factizedd as v = x * y where x and y together have the same digits as v. The smallest is 1260 = 21 * 60. But vampire numbers are just the beginning. Define: (1) Werewolf numbers: v = x * y where x and y share exactly one digit with v. (2) Ghost numbers: v = x * y where v has NO digits in common with x or y. (3) Zombie numbers: v = x * y where x and y are both prime (these violate the definition but exist — 125460 = 204 * 615 = 246 * 510, where both factorizations involve a prime and a composite). Conjecture: The density of vampire numbers in [10^{2n}, 10^{2n+1}] approaches 1/sqrt(n) as n -> infinity. Every even-length interval [10^{2k}, 10^{2k+2}] contains at least one vampire number. Ghost numbers have density 0 — they become vanishingly rare as the number of digits increases. Test: enumerate all vampire, werewolf, ghost, and zombie numbers up to 10^8. Prove the density conjecture by counting valid digit permutations. Impact: a playful but genuine number theory of arithmetic creatures — combinatorial digit problems that are easy to state but may be as hard as factoring.

Ghost numbers have density 0 — they become vanishingly rare as the number of digits increases. Test: enumerate all vampire, werewolf, ghost, and zombie numbers up to 10^8. Prove the density conjecture by counting valid digit permutations. Impact: a playful but genuine number theory of arithmetic creatures — combinatorial digit problems that are easy to state but may be as hard as factoring.
concept.lean_guess: Define vampire numbers formally: v is a vampire number iff v has 2n digits and there exist x, y each with n digits such that v = x*y and the multiset of digits of v equals the union of digits of x and y. Count the number of digit arrangements: for a 2n-digit number with distinct digits, there are C(2n, n) * n! * n! possible fang pairs, so the expected number of fang pairs is C(2n, n) * (n!)^2 / 10^{2n} = C(2n,n) / 10^n ~ 1/sqrt(n). Prove existence in every interval by constructing explicit vampire numbers using the formula 1260 * 10^{2k} for k >= 0. Test: enumerate up to 10^8.

concept.concept_description: For an orientable hypermap H defined by permutations (σ, α), a partial dual H^{E'} with respect to a hyperedge subset E' is bipartite if and only if there exists an all-crossing direction Φ of the medial map M(H) such that E' = C(Φ), provided that every hyperedge of H has even length.
concept.mathematical_framing: For an orientable hypermap H defined by permutations (σ, α), a partial dual H^{E'} with respect to a hyperedge subset E' is bipartite if and only if there exists an all-crossing direction Φ of the medial map M(H) such that E' = C(Φ), provided that every hyperedge of H has even length.
concept.lean_guess: 1. Formalize the (σ, α) model of orientable hypermaps as a pair of permutations acting transitively on a finite set. 2. Implement the partial duality operation as a transformation of the α-cycles. 3. Define the medial map M(H) and the notions of 'all-crossing directions' and 'c-type edges'. 4. Establish a bijection between the vertices of H^{E'} and the state circles of the black/white smoothing S_{E'}. 5. Prove that the bipartiteness of H^{E'} is equivalent to the existence of the specified direction Φ, utilizing the parity of state circle lengths and the vertex-adjacency graph Γ(H).
